10:# Deep Linking with Universal and App Links
14:Universal links (iOS) and App Links (Android) offer the ability to take users directly to specific content within a native app (commonly known as deep linking).
20:- Secure: Universal/App Links use HTTPS URLs that link to a website domain that you own, ensuring that no other app can use your links.
26:Here's what it looks like in practice. In this example, the user has the native app installed. They tap on app links from an email and are brought directly into the app itself. First, the root link is tapped (https://beerswift.app), which directs the user to the main app page. Next, a deep link is tapped (https://beerswift.app/tabs/tab3) bringing the user to the Tab3 page.

35:For illustrative purposes, https://beerswift.app will be used as the web app link.
41:If your website and app paths don't match, you will need to implement more advanced url pattern matching (see [this guide](https://devdactic.com/universal-links-ionic/) for examples). If your mobile app and web app use the same codebase though, this is very straightforward - just redirect to the same URL. The following examples assume this.

187:In order for Apple and Google to permit deep links to open your app, a two-way association between your website and app must be created. One file for each must be created and placed within a `.well-known` folder on your website, like so: https://beerswift.app/.well-known/.
199:First, log into the [Apple Developer site](https://developer.apple.com). Navigate to the "Certificates, Identifiers, & Profiles" section and select your app's identifier. Note the App ID Prefix (usually the same as your Team ID) and Bundle ID, and under Capabilities, toggle "Associated Domains" then save:
223:Next, upload the file to your web site (hosted on HTTPS), then validate that it's configured correctly using Apple's tool [here](https://search.developer.apple.com/appsearch-validation-tool/). The URL should follow this format: https://beerswift.app/.well-known/apple-app-site-association
227:The final step is to configure the iOS app to recognize incoming links. Open Xcode, then navigate to Signing & Capabilities. Click "+ Capability", then choose Associated Domains. In the Domains entry that appears, edit it using the format `applinks:yourdomain.com`:
255:Next, use Google's [Asset Links tool](https://developers.google.com/digital-asset-links/tools/generator) to create the Site Association file. Fill in the website domain, app package name, and SHA256 fingerprint, then click "Generate statement":

281:The final step is to configure the Android app to recognize incoming links. To do so, [add a new Intent Filter](https://developer.android.com/training/app-links/deep-linking#adding-filters) to `AndroidManifest.xml` within the `<activity>` element:

=== ch10 ===
3:A Capacitor app distributes its web bundle to every device, so every string in that bundle is public. The official audit splits the work into data, authentication and deep linking, network, and Web View security (`docs/main/guides/security.md:11-13`); the controls below follow that split. Commercial add-ons exist but are not a prerequisite (`docs/main/guides/security.md:15`).
17:For OAuth2 the return leg is a deep link, so PKCE is mandatory: verify the chosen plugin supports it before adoption (`docs/main/guides/security.md:43-45`). Auth Connect is the official PKCE-capable option (`docs/main/guides/security.md:45`). Without PKCE an intercepted authorization code can be redeemed by the attacker.
37:Read the CSP reference before tuning directives (`docs/main/guides/security.md:72`). Ordinary JavaScript hygiene still applies to the bulk of the app (`docs/main/guides/security.md:74-78`).
=== ch11 ===
18:CI runs `npm run lint` on `macos-15` after installing SwiftLint with Homebrew, and every test job depends on the lint job (`src/.github/workflows/ci.yml:33-54`). Node 22 is the CI runtime (`src/.github/workflows/ci.yml:37-39`). Local contributors on non-macOS hosts are told CI lints iOS for them (`src/CONTRIBUTING.md:68-72`).
24:ESLint extends `@ionic/eslint-config/recommended` pinned at `^0.4.0` and scans `.ts` only (`src/package.json:23`, `src/package.json:28-30`, `src/package.json:32`). The main-branch guidance names the rules that actually bite: `consistent-type-imports` (type-only imports must use `import type`, the most common failure), `explicit-module-boundary-types` on exported functions, `array-type`, `consistent-type-assertions`, `prefer-for-of`, `prefer-optional-chain`, `import/order` with groups builtin+external, parent, sibling+index alphabetised, plus `import/first`, `import/newline-after-import`, `import/no-duplicates`, `import/no-mutable-exports` (`src-head/AGENTS.md:129-143`). That same guidance warns to check the installed package before trusting a rule list…
35:An unused parameter therefore breaks compilation, not merely lint (`src-head/AGENTS.md:145-146`). `esModuleInterop`, `importHelpers`, `noEmitHelpers`, `skipLibCheck`, `declaration`, and `sourceMap` complete the options, with `target: es2017` and `module: es2015` (`src/core/tsconfig.json:2-19`).
52:Language mode is a correctness gate, not style. Tag 8.6.2 pins `SWIFT_VERSION = 5.0` across the Xcode project targets and declares `s.swift_version = '5.1'` in the podspec (`src/ios/Capacitor/Capacitor.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj:910`, `src/ios/Capacitor.podspec:23`). The main-branch guidance explains the intent: tools version 6 with `swiftLanguageModes: [.v5]`, no `async`/`await`, `actor`, `Sendable`, or `@preconcurrency`; concurrency expressed through `DispatchQueue.main.async` and the bridge's serial `dispatchQueue`, and locking via `NSLock` for shared state (`src-head/AGENTS.md:162-199`). Do not introduce Swift concurrency or flip the language mode in an unrelated change (`src-head/AGENTS.md:187-194`). Existing tag code follows GCD, e.g. the bridge's…
74:Commits follow Conventional Commits (`type(scope): subject`, with `!` after the scope for breaking changes), and Lerna enforces conventional commits for releases while restricting releases to `main` (`src-head/AGENTS.md:209-228`, `src/lerna.json:6-11`). Branch targeting is part of review: bugfixes and non-breaking work go to the stable branch, breaking work to the pre-release branch, per the current map (`src/CONTRIBUTING.md:74-84`). Large changes require prior consultation, third-party runtime dependencies require approval, and bug reports require a minimal reproduction app (`src/CONTRIBUTING.md:47-57`, `src/CONTRIBUTING.md:20-29`).
